title: The Roanoke Colony
description: England's first American colony — and the word carved into the post

concepts.title: The Colony
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1587, around 117 English colonists led by John White established a settlement on Roanoke Island, off what is now North Carolina. White returned to England later that year for supplies. War with Spain (the 1588 Armada) delayed his return.

When White finally got back to Roanoke in August 1590, the colony was empty. Houses had been dismantled. There were no signs of struggle, no graves, no bodies. The only message: the word 'CROATOAN' carved into a post, and the letters 'CRO' on a nearby tree.

concepts.title: The Croatoan Hypothesis
concepts.contentHtml:
Croatoan was the contemporary name of present-day Hatteras Island, ~80 km south of Roanoke, home to a friendly Native American people. Before sailing, White and the colonists had agreed: if they had to leave, they would carve the destination on a post — and add a Maltese cross if they were forced.

The post had 'CROATOAN' but no cross. The straightforward reading: the colonists relocated voluntarily, probably integrating into the Croatoan community. White wanted to investigate but a storm forced his ship back to England before he could land at Hatteras. He never returned.

concepts.title: Modern Evidence
concepts.contentHtml:
Recent archaeological work supports the integration hypothesis. The 'Site X' excavation in modern Bertie County (inland from Roanoke) and a separate site on Hatteras Island have produced 16th-century English artefacts in contexts consistent with European-Algonquian co-habitation: ceramic fragments, copper aglet (clothing tip), iron tools, and a sword hilt.

DNA projects have also sought descendants of the colonists, so far without conclusive results.

The 'mysterious vanishing' framing is now mostly displaced. The colonists most likely survived by integrating with the Croatoan, splitting into smaller groups, and gradually merging into the local population over several generations.

title: The Mary Celeste
description: 1872, an American merchant ship found drifting in the Atlantic

concepts.title: Discovery
concepts.contentHtml:
On 4 December 1872, the British brigantine Dei Gratia sighted a ship sailing erratically in the Atlantic between the Azores and Portugal. It was the American merchant ship Mary Celeste, missing its captain, his family, and the entire crew of 7. The ship was seaworthy, partially under sail, with adequate provisions, undisturbed cargo (1,701 barrels of denatured industrial alcohol), and no signs of struggle.

Missing: the lifeboat, the chronometer, sextant, and most of the ship's papers. The ship's daily log was still aboard; its last entry was from 25 November, nine days before the discovery.

concepts.title: What's Suggestive
concepts.contentHtml:
The cargo of denatured alcohol is the most-discussed clue. Several hundred gallons of alcohol had leaked from the barrels, building up gas pressure in the hold. Modern reconstructions: in warm weather, the leak could produce alcohol fumes that, while not flammable in the loose-stowage configuration, would have been alarming to anyone familiar with explosive risks.

A reasonable scenario: Captain Briggs, sensing a fume buildup that he feared might explode, ordered the crew into the lifeboat (with chronometer, sextant, and key papers) tied behind the ship. A sudden squall snapped the line. The Mary Celeste sailed on under partial sail; the lifeboat was lost with all hands.

concepts.title: Why It Endures
concepts.contentHtml:
The Mary Celeste case has hard-to-disprove non-mundane theories: pirates, mutiny, sea monster, mass illness, contagion. None has supporting evidence. The mundane explanation (precautionary lifeboat-deployment that went wrong) is fully consistent with all the evidence.

The case persists in folklore because the specific details — empty ship, half-eaten meal in the captain's cabin (almost certainly a 19th-century journalist's invention), still-burning lamps (also probably embellishment) — are vivid and memorable. The actual record is more boring: a partially-stocked ship with a missing crew and a plausible explanation involving a precaution gone wrong.

title: Flight 19
description: 1945: five US Navy Avengers vanish off Florida

concepts.title: The Mission
concepts.contentHtml:
On 5 December 1945, Flight 19 — five TBM Avenger torpedo bombers — took off from Naval Air Station Fort Lauderdale on a routine training run. 14 men aboard. The exercise involved a low-altitude bombing run on a small target near Bimini, then return to base.

About two hours into the flight, instructor Lt. Charles Taylor radioed that his compasses had failed and he was uncertain of his position. Over the following two hours of fragmented radio contact, Taylor's transmissions show increasing disorientation. The flight never returned. A Mariner search aircraft sent to find them also disappeared, with 13 more men aboard.

concepts.title: What Likely Happened
concepts.contentHtml:
Reconstructing from radio traffic: Taylor probably believed he was over the Florida Keys when he was actually east of Florida. He directed the flight north and east, attempting to reach Florida — but he was already over open Atlantic. Each course change took them further out to sea.

By the time they realised the error, the flight was deep over the Atlantic, fuel running low, in late-afternoon weather that was deteriorating. They almost certainly ditched in heavy seas at night. TBM Avengers were heavy aircraft that sank quickly. No wreckage has been found despite extensive subsequent searches.

The Mariner search plane probably exploded due to fuel-vapour ignition — a known problem with that aircraft type. A passing freighter reported seeing a fireball at roughly the right time and place.

concepts.title: The 'Bermuda Triangle'
concepts.contentHtml:
Flight 19 became a cornerstone of the Bermuda Triangle mythology, popularised by Charles Berlitz's 1974 bestseller. The 'triangle' (Miami–Bermuda–Puerto Rico) was framed as having anomalously high vessel and aircraft losses.

Statistical analyses by Lloyd's of London and the US Coast Guard show the Bermuda Triangle has roughly the same rate of vessel and aircraft loss as comparable busy ocean regions. The 'triangle' is a folkloric construction. The losses that did happen — Flight 19 included — generally have prosaic explanations involving weather, navigation error, and equipment failure.

title: Dyatlov Pass
description: 1959: nine experienced Soviet hikers die in the northern Urals

concepts.title: The Incident
concepts.contentHtml:
In late January 1959, a group of 10 experienced Soviet hikers led by Igor Dyatlov set out for a 14-day expedition in the northern Ural mountains. One returned early due to illness. The remaining nine never made it back.

When the search team reached their camp on a slope of Kholat Syakhl (Mansi for 'Dead Mountain'), they found the tent cut open from the inside. Tracks led downhill, made by people in socks and bare feet, in –30 °C weather. Bodies were recovered over weeks: some at a tree with broken branches at height suggesting climbing for visibility; others halfway back up the slope.

concepts.title: The Anomalies
concepts.contentHtml:
What kept the case 'unsolved' for sixty years: injuries. Several bodies showed massive internal trauma — fractured ribs, fractured skulls — without significant external bruising. One woman's tongue was missing (consistent with post-mortem scavenger activity). Some clothing had elevated radiation traces (later attributed to one hiker working in a Soviet nuclear-related facility, contaminating his clothes before the trip).

The Soviet investigation closed the case as an 'unknown compelling natural force'. This phrasing, plus the political climate, kept conspiracy theories alive: Soviet weapons tests, KGB attack, yeti, alien encounter. Most of these can be ruled out by absence of supporting evidence.

concepts.title: The 2021 Resolution
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2021, a paper in Communications Earth & Environment by Gaume and Puzrin used modern avalanche modelling to show that a small slab avalanche on the slope is consistent with all the evidence: the steep snow loading where the tent was cut, delayed onset (matching the timing), small slab volume (no wide debris field), and the type of injuries (compression by snow blocks, not external impact).

The hikers cut the tent because snow was bearing down on it. They fled downhill in panic, undressed, in extreme cold. Hypothermia did the rest. The injuries are consistent with being crushed under packed snow blocks, then partially exposed before being recovered.

Dyatlov Pass is now better explained than it was in 1959. The 'mysterious deaths' framing has largely yielded to a tragic but understandable mountaineering accident in unusual snow conditions.

title: What Vanishings Have in Common
description: Limited evidence + folklore amplification + decades of accumulation

concepts.title: The Common Pattern
concepts.contentHtml:
Every famous vanishing follows a similar trajectory: an event with limited initial evidence (small group, isolated location, poor documentation); an absence of definitive on-the-spot resolution; folklore and journalism filling in details (some real, some invented, some exaggerated); decades of repetition entrenching the 'mystery' framing; eventual modern reanalysis often producing a prosaic explanation.

This pattern doesn't mean every case is fully explained. It means most have explanations that fit normal physics and human behaviour, even when popular folklore prefers spookier readings.

concepts.title: Folklore Amplification
concepts.contentHtml:
Specific details associated with famous vanishings — half-eaten meals on the Mary Celeste, still-burning lamps, mid-conversation cut radio messages from Flight 19 — are often journalistic embellishments added years or decades after the event. They become 'facts' through repetition.

Tracing back to primary sources (period newspapers, official reports, contemporaneous correspondence) often eliminates the most striking details. The Mary Celeste's primary record is far more boring than the legend; Flight 19's transcripts have nothing as dramatic as later popular accounts claim.

concepts.title: What's Genuinely Unknown
concepts.contentHtml:
For each famous case, some details remain undetermined. We don't know exactly which Croatoan settlement specific Roanoke colonists ended up in. We don't know precisely when or where the Mary Celeste's lifeboat went down. We don't know exactly which of the Flight 19 aircraft ditched first. We don't know in detail which Dyatlov hiker was crushed by which falling snow block.

That's the actual remaining mystery: specifics within explained scenarios, not whether the scenarios themselves are correct. The famous-vanishing genre has trained audiences to expect reveals of the 'aliens did it' or 'it was murder all along' variety. The reality is that careful reconstruction usually yields plausible explanations — with the remaining uncertainty being granular detail rather than fundamental mystery.

This is consistent with how most things in the world work: less spooky than folklore, less neat than fiction, and more grounded than journalism.
